title: The spinal cord: tracts, levels and syndromes
description: Three tracts and the places where they cross account for every cord syndrome, and three independent signs locate the level.
why: Few structures in the nervous system are as predictable as the spinal cord, because three tracts and the places where they cross explain every syndrome it produces.
objectives: Draw the dorsal columns, spinothalamic tract and lateral corticospinal tract and state where each crosses.
Find the level of a cord lesion from lower motor neuron signs, reflexes and the sensory level, and explain why the sensory level can mislead.
Predict the complete, hemisection, anterior, central and posterior cord syndromes.
Distinguish conus from cauda equina lesions and recognize the signs of a tethered cord.
Recognize the cord emergencies of childhood and why they need urgent imaging of the whole spine.

sections.title: Three tracts and where they cross
sections.content:
Of all the structures in the nervous system, the spinal cord is the most obliging. It is a tube of long tracts wrapped around a column of gray matter, built the same way at every level. Three of those tracts are enough to predict almost every cord syndrome you will meet. Once you know where each of them crosses, working out a cord syndrome comes close to arithmetic.

It helps to draw all three on a single cross-section (Fisch 2012, pp. 116-117), because the syndromes can then be read straight off the drawing.

- **Dorsal columns** (vibration, joint position, fine touch). The fibers ascend **on the same side** they entered, all the way up the cord, and cross only in the lower medulla, where the next neurons form the medial lemniscus (Brazis 2011, p. 13).
- **Spinothalamic tract** (pain and temperature). The fibers synapse in the dorsal horn and **cross within a segment or two** of entering, then ascend on the opposite side.
- **Lateral corticospinal tract** (voluntary movement). These fibers have already crossed in the lower medulla, where about 75% to 90% of them decussate (Brazis 2011, p. 5). In the cord, the tract therefore runs **on the same side as the muscles it drives**.

**Putting the tracts together**

Within the cord, then, a one-sided lesion produces weakness and loss of position sense on the **same** side, below the lesion, and loss of pain and temperature on the **opposite** side, starting a little lower down. The pain and temperature loss usually starts one or two segments below the lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 106), and the simulator in this module draws it two segments down.

**Why this matters at the bedside**

A pattern that splits the modalities between the two sides, with weakness on one side and pain loss on the other, comes close to identifying the cord on its own. Nowhere else in the nervous system do the motor and pain pathways run on opposite sides of a single small structure.

**In a child**

The tracts are the same at every age, but the corticospinal tract is still myelinating in infancy, which is why an upgoing toe is normal in the first year (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam; see [[m02-the-exam|Module 2]]). In a toddler a sensory level is hard to map by questioning, so the motor signs, the reflexes and the bladder carry more of the weight.
keyPoints: The dorsal columns ascend on the same side and cross in the lower medulla (Brazis 2011, p. 13).
Spinothalamic fibers cross within one or two segments of entering the cord (Brazis 2011, p. 106).
The lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the lower medulla, so within the cord it serves the same side (Brazis 2011, p. 5).
A one-sided cord lesion causes weakness and position-sense loss on its own side below it, and pain and temperature loss on the opposite side starting a little lower.
Once the three tracts are drawn on one cross-section, the cord syndromes follow from the drawing (Fisch 2012, pp. 116-117).

question.question: A lesion destroys the left half of the spinal cord at T6. Which deficit appears on the right side of the body?
options: Weakness of the right leg
Loss of vibration and position sense in the right leg
A band of complete sensory loss at T6 on the right
Loss of pain and temperature sensation from a level a little below T6
question.explanation: Spinothalamic fibers cross within a segment or two of entering, so a left-sided lesion interrupts pain and temperature coming from the right side, starting one or two segments below the lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 106). Weakness appears on the left, because the corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla. Vibration and position loss are also on the left, because the dorsal columns are still uncrossed in the cord. The band of complete loss at the level comes from the entering roots on the side of the lesion, which is the left.

sections.title: Finding the level
sections.content:
Knowing that a lesion is in the cord is only half the job, since the scan still has to be pointed at the right segment. The cord offers three independent ways to find the level, and when they agree you can be confident.

**The reflex level**

In a cord lesion the reflexes are lost at the level of the lesion and increased below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix). With a lesion at the C5 segment, for example, the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes (C5 and C6) are lost or reduced. The triceps and finger flexor reflexes, which come from lower segments, are exaggerated (Brazis 2011, p. 12). Lower motor neuron signs at the level, meaning weakness, wasting and lost reflexes in a segmental distribution, pin the lesion to a specific segment. In the thoracic cord these signs can be subtle (Brazis 2011, p. 106).

**The sensory level, and why it can mislead**

Pinprick loss below a segmental level is the most valuable sensory sign. It is easily missed unless it is sought carefully, and sometimes repeatedly (Brazis 2011, p. 104). In complete lesions, particularly compression from outside the cord, the level on the skin may be many segments below the real lesion. A high thoracic lesion can even present with a level in the upper lumbar segments (Brazis 2011, p. 104). Band-like pain or tingling at the level of the lesion, and tenderness when the spine is tapped, may localize better (Brazis 2011, p. 104). In practice, then, imaging should run **from the sensory level upward**, and never cover the level alone.

> **Bedside trick.** An infant cannot tell you where feeling stops, but the cry can. With the baby quiet, touch a pin or an ice cube to the feet and work slowly up toward the neck, and the cry will come as the stimulus reaches the first intact dermatome (DeMyer, p. 391). At any age, move the stimulus from the numb skin toward the normal, front and back (Morris 2012, p. xxviii).

**The abdominal clues**

The abdomen offers two markers for the thoracic cord (Brazis 2011, p. 117). With a lesion at T10, the upper abdominal muscles work and the lower ones do not. When the patient lifts the head against resistance, the umbilicus is pulled upward, which is Beevor sign. The superficial abdominal reflexes are absent with a lesion above T6, although they can be hard to obtain in some healthy children, so their absence counts for less than a positive Beevor sign.

**Spinal shock**

An acute, severe cord lesion can leave the legs flaccid and areflexic at first, with the brisk reflexes and upgoing toes arriving only later (Brazis 2011, p. 106). Absent reflexes in the first days therefore do not move the lesion out of the cord.

**In a child**

The cord ends lower in a baby than in an adult. The conus sits at L3 at term and reaches the adult L1 to L2 level by about 2 months of age (Brazis 2011, p. 99). A lesion above the end of the cord gives upper motor neuron signs in the legs. Below it only roots remain, so the signs are lower motor neuron (Morris 2012, p. 29).
keyPoints: Reflexes are lost at the level of a cord lesion and brisk below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix).
Pinprick loss is the key sensory sign, but with compression it can sit many segments below the lesion, so imaging should extend upward from the level (Brazis 2011, p. 104).
Beevor sign marks T10, and the abdominal reflexes are absent with lesions above T6 (Brazis 2011, p. 117).
In spinal shock, an acute cord lesion may be flaccid and areflexic at first (Brazis 2011, p. 106).
The conus is at L3 at term and at the adult L1 to L2 level by about 2 months (Brazis 2011, p. 99).

question.question: A 15-year-old has spastic legs, brisk knee and ankle reflexes and a pinprick level at the umbilicus. An MRI of the spine at T10 is normal. What should happen next?
options: Conclude the problem is functional, since imaging at the level is normal
Image the spine above T10, because the sensory level can sit many segments below the lesion
Perform nerve conduction studies of the legs
Image the lumbar spine, below the level
question.explanation: The sensory level, especially with compression from outside the cord, can sit many segments below the true lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 104). A normal scan at the level therefore means the imaging must move upward, toward the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Spastic legs with brisk reflexes are organic upper motor neuron signs, and one normal scan is no reason to call them functional. Nerve conduction studies examine the peripheral nerves, which cannot produce spasticity or a sensory level. The lumbar spine lies below the level and cannot explain a level at the umbilicus.

sections.title: Five syndromes from one cross-section
sections.content:
Choose a level and a lesion pattern in the simulator above. The body map is computed from the three tracts, the anterior horn and the entering roots, so each syndrome below is a consequence you can check for yourself rather than an entry to memorize.

**Complete transverse lesion.** When the whole cross-section is cut, the child is weak on both sides below the lesion and has lower motor neuron signs at the level. All sensation below the level is lost, and so is control of the bladder and bowel. In a slowly developing myelopathy, urgency is the usual bladder symptom, with retention coming later. After an acute lesion the bladder is atonic at first, so retention can come early (Brazis 2011, p. 106).

**Hemisection (Brown-Séquard).** Weakness and loss of position sense appear on the side of the lesion, below it, and loss of pain and temperature appears on the opposite side, starting one or two segments down (Brazis 2011, p. 106). The usual causes are lesions outside the cord, including penetrating injuries such as stab wounds (Brazis 2011, p. 106).

**Anterior cord.** The anterior spinal artery supplies the front of the cord, so an infarct takes the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts and the anterior horns while **sparing the dorsal columns**. The child cannot move the legs or feel a pin, yet still feels the tuning fork.

**Central cord, the syrinx.** A cavity in the center of the cord first cuts the pain fibers that cross in front of it. Pain and temperature are lost over just the segments involved, often across the shoulders and arms like a cape. Sensation above and below stays normal and touch is preserved, so the loss is both dissociated and suspended. As the cavity reaches the anterior horns, the hands begin to waste. Syringomyelia is often associated with Chiari type I and II and Dandy-Walker malformations (Brazis 2011, p. 106). A syrinx in a child should therefore send you to look at the back of the skull.

**Posterior columns.** Vibration and position sense are lost below the lesion, while strength and pain sensation are kept. The child sways or falls with the eyes closed and walks on a broad base, watching the feet.

**Inside or outside the cord?**

A few clues help decide whether a lesion lies inside or outside the cord (Brazis 2011, p. 114, Table 5.11). Lesions outside the cord tend to cause early radicular and vertebral pain and early upper motor neuron signs. Lesions inside the cord tend to cause deep, poorly localized pain, prominent lower motor neuron signs, upper motor neuron signs that arrive late, and early sphincter trouble when they lie low.
keyPoints: A complete lesion removes strength and all sensation below the level, causes lower motor neuron signs at the level, and affects the bladder.
Brown-Séquard syndrome causes weakness and position-sense loss on the side of the lesion and pain loss on the opposite side, one or two segments down (Brazis 2011, p. 106).
An anterior cord lesion takes the motor and pain pathways and spares the dorsal columns.
A syrinx causes a cape-like, suspended loss of pain and temperature with touch spared, and should prompt a search for a Chiari malformation (Brazis 2011, p. 106).
Lesions outside the cord bring early radicular and vertebral pain, while lesions inside it bring prominent lower motor neuron signs and late upper motor neuron signs (Brazis 2011, p. 114).

question.question: A 12-year-old burned her hands on a stove without noticing. Pain and temperature sensation are lost over both shoulders and arms but normal on the trunk and legs; touch is normal everywhere; the small hand muscles are wasted. What should you look for next?
options: A Chiari malformation, because a central cavity (syrinx) explains the pattern
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome
A peripheral neuropathy affecting small fibers
An anterior spinal artery infarct
question.explanation: A cape of pain and temperature loss confined to a few segments, with touch spared and normal sensation above and below, is the pattern of a central cord cavity cutting the crossing pain fibers, and the hand wasting means the cavity has reached the anterior horns. Syringomyelia is associated with Chiari malformations (Brazis 2011, p. 106). Carpal tunnel syndrome would not numb the shoulders. A small-fiber neuropathy is length-dependent and would affect the feet first. An anterior spinal artery infarct causes weakness and pain loss below the lesion rather than a suspended band.

sections.title: Conus, cauda equina and the tethered cord
sections.content:
At the bottom of the cord the anatomy changes character. The cord tapers into the conus medullaris, and below it the canal holds only the bundle of lumbar and sacral roots called the cauda equina. A lesion in the conus is therefore a cord lesion, while a lesion of the cauda is a root lesion. The two sit a few centimeters apart and produce overlapping pictures, and in practice they can be hard to tell apart (Brazis 2011, p. 118).

**Conus**

Conus lesions cause early sphincter dysfunction. The bladder becomes autonomous, with no voluntary start to urination, retained urine and absent bladder sensation, and constipation is common. There may be a **symmetric saddle anesthesia**, and pain is uncommon (Brazis 2011, p. 117).

**Cauda equina**

Cauda equina lesions compress the lumbosacral roots below the L3 vertebra and cause **early radicular pain**, often one-sided or asymmetric and worse with straining (Brazis 2011, p. 118). The weakness is lower motor neuron in type, follows root distributions and comes with lost reflexes. In any patient with absent ankle reflexes, test sensation over the buttocks, because a cauda equina lesion may spare sensation elsewhere (Morris 2012, p. 29).

A common teaching shorthand says the conus gives upper motor neuron signs and the cauda gives lower motor neuron signs. Real lesions are rarely that tidy, because conus lesions often damage the nearby roots as well, so you should expect a mixture of both kinds of sign. The more reliable conus clue is early, symmetric sphincter failure with little pain.

**The tethered cord**

In a child the most important lesion in this region is a cord held too low and stretched as the spine grows. A tethered cord may present with a combination of neurologic, urologic, orthopedic and skin findings. These include numb feet, wasting of one calf or thigh, bladder and bowel trouble, foot deformities such as a high arch or clubfoot, and scoliosis. The **cutaneous markers of spinal dysraphism** are a midline hair tuft, a midline birthmark, a dermal sinus, excess hair or a fatty lump over the low back (Brazis 2011, p. 118). Many cases are associated with spina bifida occulta or a previous myelomeningocele repair (Brazis 2011, p. 118).

**At the bedside**

Undress the child enough to see the lower back, and look at the feet as well. A new high arch on one side, new wetting in a child who was dry, and a hairy patch at the base of the spine belong together.
keyPoints: A conus lesion causes early sphincter failure and symmetric saddle anesthesia with little pain (Brazis 2011, p. 117).
A cauda equina lesion causes early, asymmetric radicular pain with lower motor neuron signs in root distributions (Brazis 2011, p. 118).
In a patient with absent ankle reflexes, test sensation over the buttocks (Morris 2012, p. 29).
Conus lesions often involve the neighboring roots, so mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs are to be expected.
A tethered cord presents with bladder and bowel change, foot deformity, scoliosis and midline skin markers over the low back (Brazis 2011, p. 118).

question.question: An 8-year-old who had been dry for years has started wetting again. One foot has developed a higher arch, and there is a tuft of hair over the base of the spine. Which explanation ties these together?
options: A urinary tract infection with an unrelated foot deformity
A peroneal neuropathy
A tethered spinal cord
A behavioral regression
question.explanation: New bladder dysfunction, a foot deformity and a midline skin marker over the low back make up the urologic, orthopedic and cutaneous combination typical of a tethered cord (Brazis 2011, p. 118). The localization is the conus and lower roots, and it needs imaging. An infection could explain the wetting but not the foot or the skin marker, and treating the findings as unrelated abandons parsimony too early. A peroneal neuropathy causes foot drop, which is a different problem from a high arch with bladder change. Calling the picture behavioral ignores two objective signs.

sections.title: Cord emergencies in children
sections.content:
Delay costs more in the spinal cord than almost anywhere else in the nervous system. The cord has little room to swell, a blood supply with weak spots, and no capacity to regrow lost tracts. A cord that is compressed or inflamed can go from weak to paralyzed in hours. Some causes can be treated only while function remains, so here the localizing exam is valuable mainly for its speed.

**The usual stories**

- **Transverse myelitis** brings weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction that evolve over hours to days, sometimes after an infection and rarely after a vaccine (Brazis 2011, p. 104).
- **Compression** comes from a tumor, an abscess or a hematoma pressing from outside the cord, and back pain, tenderness when the spine is tapped, and radicular pain are its warnings (Brazis 2011, p. 104).
- **Acute flaccid myelitis** injures the gray matter, often after a viral illness, and causes flaccid, areflexic and often asymmetric weakness with little sensory loss ([[m04-motor-unit|Module 4]]).
- **Spinal cord infarct** begins suddenly, often with an anterior cord pattern.

**Three traps**

- **The reassuring reflexes.** An acute cord lesion can be flaccid and areflexic at first (Brazis 2011, p. 106). A weak child with absent reflexes who also has a sensory level or retention should be imaged as a cord lesion before anyone settles on Guillain-Barré syndrome.
- **The misleading level.** The sensory level may sit many segments below the lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 104), so the whole spine should be imaged, with the segment you suspect only the place to start.
- **The overlooked bladder.** Ask about wetting, retention and constipation, and feel for a full bladder. In a slowly developing lesion urgency usually comes first, and constipation is the commonest bowel symptom. After an acute lesion the bladder is atonic at first, so retention can come early (Brazis 2011, p. 106).

**The decision**

Back pain together with any new weakness, sensory level or bladder change in a child calls for urgent MRI of the whole spine. The exam tells the radiologist where to look first, and it should never be used to decide whether to look at all. Write the level you predict on the request and check it against the scan, because that habit is how localization skill is built.
keyPoints: The main pediatric cord emergencies are transverse myelitis, compression, acute flaccid myelitis and infarct.
Back pain, spinal tenderness and radicular pain are warnings of compression (Brazis 2011, p. 104).
An acute cord lesion can be flaccid and areflexic, so absent reflexes should not redirect the work-up to the nerves (Brazis 2011, p. 106).
Image the whole spine, because the sensory level can mislead.
Write the predicted level on the imaging request and compare it with the result.

question.question: A 6-year-old has back pain, weak floppy legs with absent reflexes, urinary retention and a pinprick level at T10, all developing over two days. What is the right next step?
options: Urgent MRI of the whole spine, because the findings point to an acute cord lesion
Nerve conduction studies for Guillain-Barré syndrome, because the reflexes are absent
Observation for 24 hours to see whether reflexes return
MRI of the brain
question.explanation: A sensory level and urinary retention point to the cord, and the absent reflexes fit spinal shock from an acute lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 106). Compression and myelitis both need urgent imaging of the whole spine, because the level may sit below the lesion. Guillain-Barré syndrome rarely produces a sensory level on the trunk, so areflexia alone should not redirect the work-up to the nerves. Waiting a day risks permanent loss if the cord is being compressed. A brain MRI does not image the cord, and a single brain lesion cannot produce a sensory level on the trunk. Brain imaging is often added once myelitis is suspected, but it never replaces imaging of the spine.

quiz.question: A teenager is stabbed in the right side of the neck at C5. Below the injury, which side of the body is weak?
options: The left side, because motor pathways cross
The right side, because the lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla
Both sides equally
Neither side; only sensation is affected in a hemisection
quiz.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract crosses in the lower medulla (Brazis 2011, p. 5), so in the cord it runs on the same side as the muscles it drives, and a right hemisection weakens the right side below the lesion. The left side is tempting because motor pathways do cross, but that crossing lies above the cord, so it explains lesions in the brain rather than a lesion below the crossing. Both sides are weak only if the lesion extends across the midline. A hemisection always involves the corticospinal tract on its own side, so strength cannot be spared.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old with sudden back pain cannot move her legs and cannot feel a pin below the umbilicus, yet she feels the tuning fork at both big toes. Which syndrome fits?
options: Complete transverse lesion
Brown-Séquard hemisection
Anterior cord syndrome
Posterior column syndrome
quiz.explanation: Loss of strength and of pain sensation with vibration preserved is the anterior cord pattern, because the anterior spinal artery supplies the front of the cord and leaves the dorsal columns intact. A complete lesion would remove vibration as well. A hemisection would split the deficits between the two sides of the body. A posterior column lesion would do the reverse, removing vibration while sparing strength and pain.

quiz.question: Which picture points to the conus medullaris rather than the cauda equina?
options: Severe one-sided radicular leg pain with late bladder trouble
Weakness in one L5 distribution only
An absent knee reflex on one side
Early urinary retention and symmetric saddle anesthesia with little pain
quiz.explanation: Early sphincter dysfunction with symmetric saddle anesthesia and little pain is the conus pattern (Brazis 2011, p. 117). Early, asymmetric radicular pain with sphincter trouble coming later is the cauda equina pattern (Brazis 2011, p. 118), so severe one-sided radicular pain with late bladder trouble describes the opposite of what the question asks for. Weakness in a single L5 distribution and a single absent knee reflex are root-level findings, which fit the cauda equina better than the conus.

quiz.question: When a 13-year-old lifts his head from the pillow against resistance, his umbilicus moves upward. Where is the cord lesion?
options: Around T10
Around T4
In the cervical cord
In the conus
quiz.explanation: Beevor sign marks a lesion at about T10, where the upper abdominal muscles still work and the lower ones do not, so the umbilicus is pulled upward (Brazis 2011, p. 117). A T4 lesion would weaken all the abdominal muscles, so nothing would pull the umbilicus preferentially in one direction. A cervical lesion would weaken the arms as well as all the abdominal muscles. A conus lesion lies below the segments that supply the abdominal muscles and leaves them intact.

quiz.question: A 16-year-old has absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes on both sides, brisk triceps reflexes and brisk knee and ankle jerks. Where is the lesion?
options: In the cervical cord at about the C5 and C6 segments
In the brain, because reflexes are brisk
In the C5 and C6 roots on both sides, with no cord involvement
In the thoracic cord
quiz.explanation: Reflexes are lost at the level of a cord lesion and increased below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix), so lost C5 and C6 reflexes with brisk C7 and leg reflexes put the lesion in the cord at C5 and C6. A brain lesion could explain the brisk reflexes but not the absent ones. Lesions of the roots alone would remove the C5 and C6 reflexes but could not make the reflexes below them brisk. A thoracic lesion would leave all the arm reflexes normal.

signOff: The resident examines a patient with a myelopathy and predicts the level before imaging, and the prediction is checked against the scan with a faculty member.

opener.parable: The spinal cord may be the most predictable structure in the nervous system. Its three long tracts cross at known places, so a lesion at a particular level and in a particular part of the cord produces a pattern you could work out on paper before you ever met the child.
opener.history: Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard (1817–1894), born in Mauritius, practiced at Queen Square and later in Paris. His name stays on the half-cut cord: weakness and lost position sense on one side, lost pain and temperature on the other.
